claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 can have an amorphous initial state after rapid quenching.
Adding 5 at% Cu to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will improve amorphous retention.
Adding 5 at% Cu to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will improve thermal stability during thermal analysis.
Cu addition will produce beneficial short-range atomic ordering in the alloy.
Short-range atomic ordering is characteristic of the amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbon.
Cu addition disrupts crystallization in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Cu addition enhances the glass-forming ability of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The Cu-modified alloy will have a crystallization temperature at least 50 K lower than the unmodified alloy.
The intervention should improve amorphous retention at cooling rates above 100 K/s.
The intervention should improve thermal stability at reheating rates below 10 K/s.
Very rapid cooling by melt spinning produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbon, whereas slower cooling produces crystalline phases.
The required Cu concentration and possible effects on mechanical strength and corrosion resistance remain uncertain.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing Cu-added and Cu-free samples using XRD, TEM, and DSC after rapid quenching and reheating.
No significant improvement combined with a crystallization-temperature reduction below 20 K is designated as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: Improved thermal stability is paired with a reduction of at least 50 K in crystallization temperature. Without another stability metric or explanation, a lower crystallization temperature normally indicates easier crystallization upon heating rather than greater thermal stability.
The prediction requires a crystallization-temperature reduction of at least 50 K, but the falsification rule only rejects reductions below 20 K, leaving outcomes from 20 K to under 50 K unresolved.
